questions.title: Identifying an Arbitrage From a Commodity Futures Mispricing
questions.prompt: A commodity trades at spot S=$80. The risk-free rate is 4%, annual storage cost is 3%, and the convenience yield is estimated at 2% (all continuously compounded), with 6 months to delivery. The quoted futures price is $82.50. Compute the fair futures price and identify whether an arbitrage opportunity exists, and if so, describe the trade.
questions.code: F_fair = S * e^((r + c - y) * T)
questions.modelAnswer: F_fair = 80 * e^((0.04+0.03-0.02)*0.5) = 80 * e^(0.05*0.5) = 80 * e^0.025 = 80 * 1.02532 ≈ $82.03. The quoted futures price of $82.50 is above the fair value of $82.03 — the futures contract is overpriced relative to the cost-of-carry model, by about $0.47 per unit. This creates a cash-and-carry arbitrage: borrow $80 at the risk-free rate, buy the commodity spot, pay the storage cost to hold it, and simultaneously sell (go short) the overpriced futures contract at $82.50. At delivery, deliver the physical commodity into the futures contract, receiving $82.50, while having spent $80 plus 6 months of financing and storage costs that the fair-value calculation already shows totals to $82.03 worth of cost — leaving a riskless profit of approximately $0.47 per unit, before accounting for any transaction costs, which in a real market would need to be smaller than this gap for the arbitrage to be worth executing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd compute the fair value first, get about $82.03, and compare it against the quoted $82.50 — the futures is overpriced, so the trade is a classic cash-and-carry: borrow to buy the physical commodity spot, hold it (paying storage), and short the overpriced future, locking in the ~$0.47 spread as a riskless profit at delivery. The one thing I'd always sanity-check before calling this a real, executable arbitrage is whether $0.47 per unit actually clears realistic transaction costs and whether the commodity can genuinely be stored and delivered as the model assumes — on paper it's riskless, but real-world frictions can easily eat a gap this size.
questions.example: F_fair ≈ $82.03 vs. quoted $82.50 — futures overpriced by about $0.47, pointing to a cash-and-carry arbitrage (buy spot, short the future).

questions.title: Demonstrating IC-Weighting Overfitting Numerically
questions.prompt: Three signals have in-sample ICs of 0.08, 0.03, and -0.01 over a 24-month window. Out-of-sample over the next 24 months, their true ICs turn out to be 0.03, 0.03, and 0.03 respectively (identical underlying quality, but noisy in-sample measurement). Explain numerically why IC-weighting based on the in-sample measurement would produce a worse out-of-sample combined signal than equal weighting here, and what this implies about when IC-weighting is and isn't worth the added complexity.
questions.modelAnswer: IC-weighting using the in-sample measurements gives weights proportional to 0.08, 0.03, and -0.01: total absolute IC = 0.08+0.03+0.01 = 0.12, so weights are 0.08/0.12≈0.667, 0.03/0.12=0.25, and -0.01/0.12≈-0.083. Applied to the true out-of-sample ICs (all 0.03), the combined signal's expected out-of-sample IC is approximately 0.667*0.03 + 0.25*0.03 + (-0.083)*0.03 = 0.03*(0.667+0.25-0.083) = 0.03*0.834 ≈ 0.025 — and worse, the negative weight on signal 3 means the combination is actively betting against a signal that's genuinely just as good as the other two, purely because it happened to measure poorly in-sample. Equal weighting (1/3 each) applied to the same true ICs of 0.03 each gives exactly 0.03, which is strictly better here. The in-sample IC differences (0.08 vs. 0.03 vs. -0.01) were pure measurement noise around a true common IC of 0.03 for all three, and the IC-weighting scheme, by trusting that noise as if it were real signal-quality information, actively degrades the combination relative to simply ignoring the (illusory) differences. This illustrates the general principle the lesson flags: IC-weighting is only worth its added complexity when the measured IC differences across signals are large and stable enough, relative to their own estimation noise, to reflect genuine, persistent quality differences — when they're actually just noise around similar true quality, equal weighting is not just simpler, it's measurably better.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the arithmetic directly: IC-weighting on the in-sample numbers gives signal 3 a negative weight, actively betting against a signal that turns out to be exactly as good as the other two — that's worse than useless, it's actively destructive. Equal weighting, by ignoring the in-sample differences entirely, gets the full 0.03 out-of-sample IC rather than the roughly 0.025 (or worse) the IC-weighted version delivers. The lesson here isn't 'never use IC-weighting' — it's that IC-weighting is only earning its complexity when the measured differences between signals are large and stable relative to their own noise, and this example is constructed specifically to show what happens when they aren't.

questions.title: Resizing a Volatility-Targeted Position After a GARCH Forecast Change
questions.prompt: A volatility-targeting strategy holds a position sized so expected annualized risk contribution is 10%. Yesterday's GARCH forecast implied annualized volatility of 16%. Today's updated forecast implies annualized volatility of 28%. Compute the required change in position size, and explain why a strategy that instead resized based on trailing 60-day historical volatility would likely react too slowly here.
questions.modelAnswer: Volatility targeting sizes a position inversely to forecast volatility: if yesterday's position was sized to hit a 10% risk contribution using a 16% volatility forecast, the position size was proportional to 1/0.16 = 6.25. Today's position, using the updated 28% forecast, should be proportional to 1/0.28 ≈ 3.571. The ratio of new to old position size is 3.571/6.25 ≈ 0.571 — the position needs to be cut by roughly 43% to keep the risk contribution at the same 10% target, since volatility rose by a factor of 1.75 (28/16) and position size must fall by the same proportional factor to offset it exactly. A 60-day trailing historical volatility estimate would react far more slowly here because it averages in 59 days of calmer pre-spike volatility alongside the first day or two of the new, higher-volatility regime — it would take many days for the rolling window to fully reflect the new, higher volatility level, during which the position would remain oversized relative to the strategy's actual current risk target. GARCH's conditional variance, by contrast, reacts to the most recent shock immediately (through the alpha term) and carries forward a persistent elevated level (through the beta term), which is exactly why it resizes the position appropriately in a single step rather than gradually catching up over weeks.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd size this as inverse-proportional to volatility: the forecast jumped from 16% to 28%, a factor of 1.75, so the position needs to shrink by the reciprocal of that factor, roughly 43%, to keep the risk contribution at its 10% target. A 60-day trailing historical volatility estimate would badly lag this move — it would still be mostly reflecting the calmer pre-spike period for weeks, leaving the position oversized relative to actual current risk exactly during the window that matters most. That lag is the direct, practical argument for using a GARCH-based forecast rather than a simple rolling-window estimate for volatility-targeted sizing.

questions.title: A GARCH Model Persistently Underforecasting Ahead of a Regime Change
questions.prompt: A GARCH(1,1) model with alpha=0.08 and beta=0.90 has, for the past month, consistently underforecast next-day volatility by a wide margin, right as the market has entered a sustained period of structurally higher volatility. Diagnose why this specific model is struggling here, and what you'd change.
questions.modelAnswer: With alpha+beta=0.98, this model is highly persistent but mean-reverts, by design, toward its estimated long-run unconditional variance — a variance level estimated over a historical window that mostly reflects the calmer regime before the current shift. During a genuine, sustained regime change to structurally higher volatility, every one-step-ahead forecast, even though it reacts somewhat to the latest shock via alpha, is still being pulled by beta's persistence term back toward that stale, too-low long-run average, which produces a systematic, one-directional underforecast that persists for as long as the model's underlying long-run variance estimate hasn't been re-estimated on fresher data. This is different from and worse than ordinary forecast noise, because it's a structural, one-sided bias rather than random forecast error scattered in both directions — the diagnostic signature of exactly this problem is that the forecast errors are consistently one-sided (always too low) rather than zero-mean and symmetric. The fix isn't simply re-estimating the same GARCH(1,1) specification on the same long window, since that would still blend the old and new regimes together; it requires either re-estimating the model on a more recent window that better reflects the new regime, or switching to a regime-switching volatility model that can represent a discrete shift in the long-run variance level explicitly, or at minimum supplementing the GARCH forecast with a shorter-window realized volatility check specifically to catch exactly this kind of systematic, persistent underforecast before it compounds into underpriced VaR or position sizing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The tell here is that the errors are one-sided, not just noisy — that's a different and more serious problem than ordinary forecast imprecision. This model's high persistence (alpha+beta=0.98) means every forecast is still being pulled toward a long-run variance estimated mostly from the calmer regime before this shift, so it will keep underforecasting for as long as that stale long-run estimate hasn't caught up. I wouldn't just re-fit the same specification on the same long window — I'd re-estimate on a more recent window that actually reflects the new regime, or move to a model that can represent a discrete regime shift explicitly, and in the meantime I'd cross-check the GARCH forecast against a shorter realized-volatility window to catch this kind of systematic bias early.

questions.title: Live Sharpe Collapsing Due to an Unrealistic Fill Assumption
questions.prompt: A strategy backtested with a 'fills at next-bar close' assumption shows a Sharpe of 1.8. Once live, using real next-bar-open fills, the realized Sharpe is 0.4. Diagnose exactly what the backtest smuggled in, and why the gap is this large specifically for this strategy's design.
questions.modelAnswer: A 'fills at next-bar close' assumption, when the signal was generated from that same bar's own close, smuggles in a full extra bar's worth of price movement the strategy could never have actually observed before trading — the backtest is implicitly assuming the strategy can trade at a price that isn't even known until the end of the very bar it's trading on, which is exactly as physically impossible as fills at the signal bar's own close. This is a disguised form of lookahead bias specifically in the execution layer rather than the signal layer, and it tends to produce an inflated Sharpe whose magnitude depends on how much of the strategy's apparent edge was actually coming from that extra, illegitimate bar of foresight rather than genuine predictive signal. The size of the gap here — 1.8 down to 0.4 — suggests this strategy's measured edge was substantially inflated by this specific assumption, meaning a meaningful share of what looked like real predictive power was actually just the backtest quietly letting the strategy react to information (the next bar's full price path) it could never have had in real time. The correct fill convention for a signal generated at bar N's close is a fill at bar N+1's open, the earliest price actually observable and tradeable after the signal is known — and the fact that switching to this correct convention alone (separately from transaction costs or slippage, which would make the gap even larger) collapses the Sharpe this much indicates the strategy's true edge, once honestly measured, may not be much above the risk-free hurdle.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is lookahead bias wearing a different costume — fills at next-bar close instead of next-bar open quietly hands the strategy a full bar of price movement it couldn't have known about before trading, which is just as illegitimate as fills at the same bar's own close. A collapse from 1.8 to 0.4 after fixing just the fill convention, before even layering in slippage and transaction costs, tells me a large share of the original 'edge' was this specific artifact, not real predictive signal — and I'd want to know the true number including realistic costs on top of the corrected fill convention before drawing any further conclusions about whether this strategy has a real edge at all.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing 'fills at next-bar close' as a disguised form of lookahead bias in the execution layer
Treating the gap as simply 'the backtest wasn't perfect' rather than identifying the specific, named mechanism
Not connecting the magnitude of the collapse to how much of the apparent edge was an artifact of this one assumption
Forgetting that transaction costs and slippage, layered on top of the corrected fill convention, would likely widen the gap further
keyPoints: 'Fills at next-bar close' smuggles in a full bar of unknowable future price movement, a disguised lookahead bias
The correct convention is a fill at next-bar open, the earliest actually-observable, tradeable price after the signal
The large magnitude of the collapse (1.8 to 0.4) suggests much of the apparent edge was this specific artifact
Realistic slippage and transaction costs on top of the corrected fill convention would likely widen the gap further

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the fill assumption as a disguised lookahead bias
Correctly states the proper fill convention
Correctly interprets the magnitude of the collapse
Notes that further realistic costs would likely widen the gap

questions.title: A Risk-Parity Book Blowing Up as Correlations Spike
questions.prompt: A risk-parity portfolio, constructed using inverse-volatility weights estimated from a 60-day rolling window of calm-period data, suffers losses far larger than its target risk level during a sudden market-wide selloff where every asset's correlation with every other asset spikes toward one. Diagnose the specific flaw in the construction process.
questions.modelAnswer: Inverse-volatility weighting, as a construction method, only accounts for each asset's own standalone volatility — it says nothing about how assets move together, which means it implicitly assumes the portfolio's diversification benefit from imperfect correlation will hold going forward, without ever explicitly modeling or stress-testing that assumption. During a calm period, the 60-day rolling correlations between the assets may have been low or even negative, making the inverse-volatility-weighted combination appear to achieve a modest, well-diversified total risk level. The moment a market-wide selloff hits and correlations spike toward one — a known, common pattern tied to the same correlation-to-one mechanism that affects equity long/short books — the portfolio's actual combined volatility jumps sharply above what the inverse-volatility weights alone would suggest, because the diversification benefit that the weighting scheme implicitly assumed, but never explicitly modeled via a full covariance matrix, has simply disappeared. The specific flaw: true risk parity requires sizing positions by each asset's marginal contribution to total portfolio risk computed from the full covariance matrix (including cross-asset correlations), not merely by inverse standalone volatility, which is only a valid shortcut for risk parity when correlations are low and stable — an assumption that is precisely false during the kind of stress event where risk management matters most.
questions.professionalAnswer: The specific flaw is that inverse-volatility weighting is being used as a shortcut for risk parity, and that shortcut only works when cross-asset correlations are low and stable — which is exactly the condition that breaks during a market-wide selloff. The calm-period 60-day window baked in low correlations that simply don't hold anymore once everything starts moving together, and because the construction never used the full covariance matrix to size risk contributions explicitly, it had no way to see this coming. True risk parity needs marginal risk contribution from the full covariance matrix, not just each asset's own standalone volatility — and that's the fix.
commonMistakes: Blaming the specific assets chosen rather than the construction methodology itself
Not recognizing inverse-volatility weighting as only a valid risk-parity shortcut under the low-correlation assumption
Missing the direct connection to the correlation-to-one mechanism seen elsewhere during market-wide shocks
Not proposing the correct fix (full covariance-matrix-based marginal risk contribution) rather than just a different lookback window
keyPoints: Inverse-volatility weighting ignores cross-asset correlation entirely, only sizing by standalone volatility
This is a valid risk-parity shortcut only when correlations are low and stable, an assumption baked in from the calm estimation period
A market-wide selloff spikes correlations toward one, destroying the assumed diversification benefit
True risk parity requires marginal risk contribution computed from the full covariance matrix, not just standalone volatility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the construction methodology's flaw, not the specific assets
Correctly explains why inverse-volatility weighting is only a valid shortcut under low correlation
Connects the failure to the correlation-to-one pattern during market shocks
Proposes the correct fix (full covariance-based risk contribution)

questions.title: A Fama-MacBeth Risk Premium That Flips Sign Across Sub-Periods
questions.prompt: A Fama-MacBeth estimate of a factor's risk premium is positive and marginally significant over a full 20-year sample, but splitting the sample into four 5-year sub-periods shows the period-by-period lambda_t estimates alternating between strongly positive and strongly negative. Diagnose what this instability implies, and what you'd tell a PM who wants to size a position based on the full-sample estimate.
questions.modelAnswer: The sub-period instability is itself exactly the information the Fama-MacBeth standard error is designed to capture, and it's worth being explicit that this isn't a separate problem on top of Fama-MacBeth's standard framework — the full-sample standard error already reflects, by construction, how much the period-by-period lambda_t bounces around across the entire 20-year history, including whatever instability is visible when you split it into sub-periods. A marginally significant full-sample average sitting on top of alternating strongly-positive and strongly-negative sub-period estimates is a strong sign the 'true' risk premium is not stable over time — it may be regime-dependent (compensated during certain economic conditions and penalized during others) rather than a constant, persistently-positive risk premium the way a textbook factor model implicitly assumes. Telling a PM to size a position based on the full-sample point estimate alone, without flagging this sub-period instability, risks presenting a borderline-significant, time-varying effect as if it were a reliable, stable source of return — when the more honest read is that the premium's sign itself may depend on conditions that need to be identified and conditioned on, not averaged away into one number. The right recommendation: investigate whether the sub-period flips correlate with an identifiable macro or market regime variable; if they do, the premium should be sized conditionally on that regime, not as a flat, always-on exposure; if no such explanation is found, the marginal full-sample significance combined with this degree of instability argues for a smaller, more cautious position size than the raw point estimate alone would suggest.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the PM directly that a marginally significant full-sample average sitting on top of sub-periods that flip between strongly positive and strongly negative isn't really describing one stable risk premium — it's averaging together what might be two or more genuinely different regimes. Before sizing anything off the full-sample number, I'd want to know whether those sub-period flips line up with an identifiable macro regime; if they do, size the position conditionally on that regime rather than as a flat, always-on bet, and if they don't, the honest conclusion is that this result is less trustworthy than the marginal significance on its own makes it look, and the position should be sized more conservatively.
commonMistakes: Treating the sub-period instability as a separate issue from what Fama-MacBeth's standard error is already designed to capture
Recommending the PM size off the full-sample point estimate without flagging the instability at all
Not proposing investigating whether the flips correlate with an identifiable regime variable
Concluding the premium is simply 'not real' rather than considering it might be genuinely regime-dependent
keyPoints: Sub-period instability is exactly what the Fama-MacBeth standard error is designed to reflect, not a separate problem
Alternating strongly positive/negative sub-periods suggest a regime-dependent, not stable, risk premium
Sizing off the full-sample point estimate alone risks treating an unstable effect as a reliable one
Investigate whether instability correlates with an identifiable regime; size conditionally or more conservatively

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the relationship between sub-period instability and the FM standard error
Correctly interprets the instability as suggesting a regime-dependent premium
Gives the PM an honest, non-alarmist but appropriately cautious recommendation
Proposes investigating a regime correlation as a concrete next step

questions.title: Diagnosing a Funding-Liquidity-to-Market-Liquidity Spiral
questions.prompt: A fund facing investor redemptions is forced to sell positions to raise cash, but the positions it sells cheapest and fastest are its most liquid holdings, leaving it progressively more concentrated in illiquid assets even as its NAV keeps falling. Diagnose the spiral mechanism at work and what structural decision created this vulnerability.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the classic interaction between funding liquidity risk and market liquidity risk reinforcing each other in a spiral. The fund's redemption pressure is a funding liquidity problem — needing cash to meet obligations (investor withdrawals) regardless of whether the fund is otherwise solvent. Facing that pressure, the fund rationally sells its most liquid holdings first, since those can be sold fastest and with the least market impact — but doing so repeatedly, redemption after redemption, mechanically shifts the portfolio's composition toward a higher concentration of illiquid assets over time, even without the fund manager intending that outcome. This creates a market liquidity risk problem that compounds the original funding problem: as the portfolio becomes more concentrated in illiquid holdings, any future redemption requires selling into thinner, harder-to-exit markets, at a larger market-impact cost and often at a further-depressed price, which can itself trigger further investor redemptions if the resulting NAV decline alarms remaining investors — a feedback loop where meeting funding liquidity needs degrades market liquidity, which in turn worsens the fund's apparent performance and funding pressure. The structural decision that created this vulnerability is the fund's redemption terms themselves: offering investors more frequent or larger redemption rights than the underlying portfolio's actual liquidity profile can comfortably support, a basic liquidity mismatch between the fund's liabilities (redeemable on demand or short notice) and its assets (including meaningfully illiquid holdings) that doesn't show up as a problem until redemption pressure actually arrives.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd name this as the funding-liquidity-to-market-liquidity feedback loop directly: redemption pressure (funding liquidity) forces selling the most liquid assets first, which mechanically concentrates the remaining book into illiquid holdings, which then makes any future redemption more expensive and value-destructive (market liquidity), which can trigger more redemptions — a genuine spiral, not a sequence of unrelated bad luck. The root structural cause isn't any individual trade, it's the original mismatch between how liquid the fund promised investors it would be (its redemption terms) and how liquid its underlying assets actually are — and that mismatch is invisible until redemption pressure actually tests it.
commonMistakes: Diagnosing this as a series of individually bad trading decisions rather than a structural funding/market liquidity spiral
Not explaining why selling the most liquid assets first mechanically worsens the portfolio's remaining liquidity profile
Missing the feedback-loop aspect where market liquidity deterioration can trigger further redemptions
Not identifying the original asset-liability liquidity mismatch (redemption terms vs. underlying asset liquidity) as the root structural cause
keyPoints: Redemption pressure is a funding liquidity problem independent of the fund's underlying solvency
Selling the most liquid assets first to meet it mechanically concentrates the remaining portfolio in illiquid holdings
This degrades market liquidity for future redemptions, which can trigger further redemptions, forming a spiral
The root structural cause is a mismatch between redemption terms offered and the underlying portfolio's actual liquidity profile

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the funding-to-market liquidity spiral mechanism
Correctly explains why selling liquid assets first worsens the remaining portfolio's liquidity
Correctly explains the feedback-loop/further-redemption risk
Correctly identifies the structural redemption-terms mismatch as the root cause

questions.title: A Market Maker's Inventory Risk Spiraling During One-Sided Flow
questions.prompt: A market maker's inventory in a stock grows from flat to a large net short position over a single trading session, as customer buy orders consistently outpace sell orders despite the market maker repeatedly widening and skewing its quotes. Diagnose why the standard inventory-skew response isn't containing the risk here, and what else should be done.
questions.modelAnswer: Skewing the quote (tightening the offer side and widening the bid side, to discourage further customer buying and encourage selling back) is the standard tool for managing inventory risk when order flow is noise-driven and roughly balanced over time — it works by making the market maker's own side of the trade progressively less attractive as inventory builds, nudging flow back toward neutral. If customer buy orders keep outpacing sells even as the quote is repeatedly skewed more aggressively, that's a strong signal the order flow isn't noise at all — it's informed, directional flow, meaning a meaningful share of the market is trading on information the market maker doesn't have, and simply widening the spread or skewing further is fighting a losing, continually-retreating battle rather than addressing the actual problem, since a genuinely better-informed counterparty will keep buying even at a worse price if they believe the stock is headed meaningfully higher. At this point, the inventory-risk-management playbook built for noise-driven flow has effectively reached its limits, and the market maker needs to treat this as an adverse-selection event rather than an ordinary inventory-management problem: this likely means pulling back from continuously quoting altogether for a period (reducing size or temporarily widening to levels that stop attracting flow entirely, rather than trying to find a skew that still trades), and separately, hedging the accumulated short position directly in a correlated, more liquid instrument (an index future or an options position) rather than relying solely on the inventory-skew mechanism to eventually bring the position back to flat through its own trading activity.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that skewing isn't working is itself the diagnostic signal — that only happens when the flow isn't noise, it's informed, and a market maker can't out-skew a counterparty who's willing to keep buying at a worse price because they believe they know something real. At that point I'd stop treating this as routine inventory management and start treating it as an adverse-selection event: pull back from quoting meaningfully, or stop altogether for a period, and hedge the accumulated position directly in a correlated, liquid instrument rather than waiting for the skew to eventually work its way back to flat on its own.
commonMistakes: Recommending further skewing or widening as if the flow were still noise-driven
Not recognizing persistent one-sided flow despite aggressive skewing as the signature of informed, not noise, flow
Treating this purely as an inventory problem rather than an adverse-selection event requiring a different response
Not proposing a direct hedge in a correlated instrument as part of the response
keyPoints: Quote skewing is designed for noise-driven, roughly balanced flow, not persistent, informed directional flow
Flow that keeps outpacing an increasingly aggressive skew is the signature of informed, adverse-selection-driven trading
At that point, continuing to widen/skew is fighting a losing battle rather than addressing the real problem
The correct response: pull back from quoting and hedge the accumulated position directly in a correlated, liquid instrument

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why standard inventory skewing isn't working here
Correctly identifies informed/adverse-selection flow as the underlying cause
Proposes pulling back from quoting as part of the response
Proposes a direct hedge in a correlated instrument

questions.title: A Carry Strategy's Sharpe Halving Under Realistic Turnover
questions.prompt: An FX carry strategy that rebalances weekly shows a cost-free backtested Sharpe of 1.3. Once realistic transaction costs and bid-ask spread crossing are applied, the Sharpe drops to 0.65 — exactly half. Explain what this specific ratio (exactly half, not collapsed to near zero) implies about the strategy, in contrast to the earlier case of a daily-rebalanced strategy whose Sharpe collapsed from 2.2 to 0.3.
questions.modelAnswer: The key diagnostic is the magnitude of the degradation relative to turnover, not just the fact that costs reduced the Sharpe. A weekly-rebalanced strategy pays its round-trip cost roughly 52 times a year, meaningfully less often than a daily-rebalanced strategy's roughly 252 times a year — so for a comparable per-trade cost, the weekly strategy's total annual cost drag is structurally much smaller, which is consistent with a cost impact that dents the Sharpe meaningfully (cutting it in half) without eliminating it. This is a fundamentally healthier signature than the daily strategy's collapse from 2.2 to 0.3: a Sharpe halving while remaining a still-respectable 0.65 suggests the carry strategy's underlying edge was genuinely larger relative to its (lower) trading frequency, and real, durable trading costs, while a legitimate and material drag worth continuing to minimize, haven't eliminated the edge entirely. By contrast, the earlier daily strategy's near-total collapse indicated its apparent edge was largely a turnover-driven illusion in the first place. This carry strategy's result is more consistent with carry's own known economic story — it's compensation for a real, persistent risk premium (as established in the interest-rate-parity discussion), which should be expected to survive reasonable transaction costs, in contrast to a thin, noise-driven signal that only looked good because costs were originally assumed away entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail I'd focus on is that this Sharpe was cut in half, not collapsed toward zero — and the reason that's meaningfully different from the earlier daily strategy's near-total wipeout is turnover: weekly rebalancing pays its round-trip cost about a fifth as often as daily rebalancing, so a comparable per-trade cost produces a much smaller total annual drag. A carry strategy surviving costs at a still-respectable 0.65 Sharpe is consistent with carry's own economic story — a real, persistent risk premium, not a thin signal that only looked good when costs were ignored — and that's a genuinely more reassuring result than the daily strategy's collapse was.
commonMistakes: Treating any cost-driven Sharpe reduction as equally concerning, without comparing the magnitude to the strategy's trading frequency
Not explaining why weekly rebalancing's lower turnover produces a structurally smaller annual cost drag than daily rebalancing
Missing the contrast with the earlier daily-strategy example as the point of the comparison
Not connecting the result to carry's own economic story as a persistent, cost-surviving risk premium
keyPoints: Weekly rebalancing incurs its round-trip cost roughly 52 times a year versus daily's roughly 252 times
A Sharpe halving while remaining a still-respectable 0.65 is a fundamentally healthier signature than a near-total collapse
This suggests the carry strategy's underlying edge is genuinely larger relative to its trading frequency, not a turnover-driven illusion
The result is consistent with carry's own economic story as a real, persistent, cost-surviving risk premium

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly connects turnover frequency to the magnitude of cost drag
Correctly contrasts this result with the earlier daily-strategy collapse
Correctly interprets what a surviving Sharpe implies about the underlying edge
Connects the result to carry's own economic rationale as a persistent risk premium

questions.title: Designing a Research Pipeline That Governs Against Overfitting End-to-End
questions.prompt: Design a research pipeline, from initial idea through to approved-for-capital signal, for a team of researchers, with explicit governance checkpoints that prevent overfitting from creeping in at any single stage: hypothesis formation, signal combination, and portfolio construction.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd architect this as a staged pipeline with a mandatory, timestamped artifact and a hard data-access boundary at each stage, not just informal best practices. Stage one, hypothesis formation: every new idea must produce a written, timestamped hypothesis document — universe, exact signal definition, expected direction and magnitude, success metric, and kill criteria — committed to a version-controlled log before any code touches live data, exactly as the from-idea-to-hypothesis discipline requires; the pipeline should technically prevent a researcher from running a backtest against a hypothesis that hasn't been logged first. Stage two, signal combination: any combination weights (equal, IC-based, or otherwise) must be estimated only on a designated training partition of the data, with the held-out validation partition's existence enforced at the infrastructure level — the backtest engine itself should refuse to compute or report a result on the validation partition until the combination weights from the training partition are frozen and logged. Stage three, portfolio construction: any estimated inputs (expected returns, covariance structure) feeding an optimizer should similarly be fit only on the training partition, with position constraints and/or shrinkage applied by default rather than optional, specifically because unconstrained mean-variance optimization is known to overfit estimation noise into extreme weights. Finally, a single, final out-of-sample test — genuinely never touched by any researcher at any earlier stage, for any signal — is the only basis on which a signal is approved for live capital, and the pipeline should log and report exactly how many signals, parameter variations, and combination schemes were tried across the whole process, since that number is itself necessary context for judging how much to trust the final result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this so that each stage's defense against overfitting is enforced by the infrastructure itself, not left to researcher discipline: a hypothesis has to be logged and timestamped before any backtest can run against it, combination weights and portfolio-construction inputs can only be computed from a training partition the system itself walls off from the validation partition until weights are frozen, and a single, genuinely untouched final out-of-sample period is the only gate for approving live capital. I'd also have the pipeline automatically log how many signals and variations were tried in total, because that count is necessary context for anyone judging how much to trust whatever made it through to the end.
commonMistakes: Relying on researcher discipline or documentation alone rather than infrastructure-enforced data partitioning
Not applying the same train/validation discipline consistently across all three stages (hypothesis, combination, construction)
Leaving mean-variance optimization unconstrained by default rather than defaulting to position caps or shrinkage
Not logging the total number of signals/variations tried across the whole pipeline as context for the final result
keyPoints: Every hypothesis must be logged and timestamped before any backtest runs against it
Signal-combination weights are computed only on a training partition, with validation data infrastructure-walled off until weights are frozen
Portfolio-construction inputs are fit only on the training partition, with default position constraints/shrinkage
A single, genuinely untouched final out-of-sample test gates live-capital approval, with the total number of variations tried logged

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs infrastructure-enforced hypothesis logging
Correctly designs train/validation separation for signal combination
Correctly designs train/validation separation and default constraints for portfolio construction
Proposes a final, untouched out-of-sample gate with variation-count logging

questions.title: Designing a Firm-Wide GARCH-Based Dynamic Risk System
questions.prompt: Design a firm-wide risk system that uses GARCH-family volatility forecasts to drive both daily VaR reporting and volatility-targeted position sizing across multiple desks, with appropriate safeguards against model risk.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd architect this with a shared volatility-forecasting service as the single source of truth, rather than each desk independently fitting its own GARCH models, so that VaR reporting and position sizing are always using consistent, reconciled volatility estimates. This service would fit a GARCH-family model (with an asymmetric extension like GJR-GARCH for equities, given the leverage effect) per instrument or risk factor on a defined re-fitting cadence, publish the resulting conditional variance forecasts to a shared feed, and version every forecast so any VaR number or position-sizing decision made on a given day can be traced back to the exact model parameters and forecast that drove it. The daily VaR reporting layer consumes this feed directly, computing parametric VaR per desk and firm-wide, aggregated with the firm's actual covariance structure rather than naive summation. The position-sizing layer, for any desk running volatility-targeted strategies, consumes the same feed to resize positions inversely to forecast volatility, guaranteeing the risk numbers being reported and the actual position sizes being held are always derived from the identical underlying forecast, never two independently-computed, potentially inconsistent numbers. For model-risk safeguards: every forecast is continuously back-tested against subsequently realized volatility (the standard RMSE-against-realized-vol check), with an automated alert if forecast errors become persistently one-sided (the signature of a stale or regime-blind model); a naive historical-volatility benchmark is computed in parallel at all times, not as a replacement but as a sanity check, triggering a manual review if the GARCH forecast and the naive benchmark diverge beyond a defined tolerance; and the model's fitted parameters are reviewed on a fixed schedule by someone independent of the desk using the forecasts, consistent with the three-lines-of-defense principle.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design principle I'd insist on is one shared volatility-forecasting service feeding both VaR and position sizing, not two independently-built pipelines that could quietly disagree with each other. I'd use an asymmetric GARCH variant for equities given the leverage effect, version every forecast for full traceability, and build in model-risk safeguards as first-class features, not afterthoughts: continuous back-testing against realized volatility with an alert on persistent one-sided errors, a parallel naive benchmark that triggers manual review on divergence, and an independent, scheduled review of the model's fitted parameters — because a dynamic risk system that silently drifts wrong is more dangerous than a static one everyone already knows to distrust.
commonMistakes: Allowing each desk to fit its own independent GARCH model rather than a single shared forecasting service
Not using an asymmetric GARCH variant despite the leverage effect being specifically relevant for equities
Treating VaR reporting and position sizing as separate pipelines rather than both consuming the same versioned forecast
Omitting concrete model-risk safeguards such as continuous back-testing, a parallel naive benchmark, and independent review
keyPoints: A single, shared, versioned volatility-forecasting service feeds both VaR reporting and position sizing
An asymmetric GARCH variant (e.g., GJR-GARCH) is appropriate given the leverage effect, particularly for equities
Firm-wide VaR aggregation should use the actual covariance structure, not naive summation
Model-risk safeguards: continuous back-testing against realized volatility, a parallel naive benchmark, and independent scheduled review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a single shared, versioned forecasting service
Correctly connects VaR reporting and position sizing to the same forecast feed
Proposes appropriate model choice (asymmetric GARCH) and aggregation method
Proposes concrete, multi-layered model-risk safeguards

questions.title: Designing Exotic Derivatives Pricing Infrastructure
questions.prompt: Design a pricing infrastructure for a derivatives desk that trades vanilla options, American options, Asian options, and barrier options, choosing the appropriate numerical method for each payoff type and explaining how the system should validate its own outputs.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd route each instrument type to a different pricing engine based on its specific payoff structure, rather than forcing one universal method to handle everything. Vanilla European options go to a closed-form Black-Scholes engine, the fastest and most precise option when it applies. American options go to a binomial or trinomial tree engine, since the tree's node-by-node hold-versus-exercise comparison naturally produces the early-exercise boundary without needing a separate algorithm. Asian and other strongly path-dependent payoffs go to a Monte Carlo engine, since their value depends on the whole simulated price path rather than a single terminal value or a cleanly collapsible lattice. Barrier options are a genuinely mixed case architecturally: for simple, single-barrier structures under standard Black-Scholes assumptions, a semi-closed-form solution exists and should be used for speed and precision; for more complex or multi-barrier structures, the system should fall back to Monte Carlo (for a continuously-monitored barrier) or a finite-difference PDE solver (which handles barriers as a boundary condition directly and efficiently). Critically, I'd build cross-validation into the system itself rather than trusting any one engine's output in isolation: every new pricing engine, before being trusted in production, must reproduce the closed-form Black-Scholes price on the vanilla European case as a sanity check (tree, Monte Carlo, and PDE methods should all converge to the Black-Scholes price as their respective approximation parameters — tree steps, simulation paths, grid resolution — are increased), and every Monte Carlo-based price should report alongside it a standard error from the simulation, with a defined minimum path count required before a price is considered trustworthy enough to trade on, rather than returning a single point estimate with no indication of its own numerical uncertainty.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd route by payoff structure, not force one method to do everything: closed-form for vanilla, trees for American exercise (since the early-exercise boundary falls out of the same algorithm automatically), Monte Carlo for path-dependent payoffs like Asian options, and a mix of semi-closed-form or Monte Carlo/PDE for barriers depending on complexity. The non-negotiable safeguard I'd build in is convergence validation — every new engine has to reproduce the known Black-Scholes price on the vanilla case as its numerical parameters are increased — and every Monte Carlo price needs to report its own simulation standard error alongside the point estimate, so nobody trades off a number whose own uncertainty nobody checked.
commonMistakes: Using one universal pricing method for all instrument types rather than routing by payoff structure
Not recognizing that a tree naturally produces the American early-exercise boundary without a separate algorithm
Omitting a validation step that checks new engines against known closed-form results
Returning a Monte Carlo price without reporting its simulation standard error alongside it
keyPoints: Route each instrument type to the appropriate engine: closed-form, tree, Monte Carlo, or PDE, based on payoff structure
Trees handle American exercise naturally through node-by-node hold-vs-exercise comparison
Barrier options may use semi-closed-form, Monte Carlo, or PDE methods depending on complexity
Validate every engine against known closed-form results, and report Monte Carlo standard error alongside every simulated price

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly routes each instrument type to an appropriate pricing method
Correctly explains why trees naturally handle American exercise
Correctly addresses barrier option complexity tiers
Proposes concrete validation safeguards (convergence checks, simulation standard error)

questions.title: Designing an Execution Architecture With Partial-Fill Awareness
questions.prompt: Design an execution architecture for a strategy running near its estimated capacity ceiling, where large limit orders routinely only partially fill within a trading session. The architecture must correctly account for partial fills in both the backtester and the live execution system.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd design the backtester's fill-simulation layer to explicitly model partial fills rather than assuming binary filled-or-not outcomes: for a limit order, the simulator should check the bar's actual traded volume at or through the limit price, and only mark as filled the portion of the order size that the available liquidity could plausibly have absorbed, carrying the unfilled remainder forward to subsequent bars rather than assuming the full size always executes once the limit is touched. This matters specifically for a capacity-constrained strategy because assuming full fills when the strategy is already near its capacity ceiling would materially overstate how much of the intended position the strategy could actually build, and therefore overstate its realistic backtested returns. The live execution system needs the mirror-image logic: when a submitted order partially fills, the system must track the remaining unfilled quantity explicitly as its own state, decide whether to resubmit the remainder immediately, resubmit at an adjusted price, or hold it for the next session, and feed the actual realized participation rate back into a monitoring component that compares it against the model's assumed capacity ceiling — if live partial-fill rates are consistently worse than the backtester assumed, that's a direct, measurable signal the strategy's true capacity is lower than modeled, and sizing should be adjusted down in response rather than continuing to trade the originally-modeled size. Both the backtester and the live system should share the same underlying partial-fill logic and capacity assumptions wherever possible, specifically so a live capacity breach gets detected by comparing against the same model the backtest was built on, not two inconsistent capacity models that could silently disagree.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd make partial fills a first-class concept in both systems, not an edge case: the backtester's limit-order logic should only credit the portion of size the bar's actual liquidity could have absorbed, carrying the rest forward — assuming full fills near a capacity ceiling would materially overstate the strategy's realistic returns. The live system needs to track unfilled remainders explicitly and decide how to handle them, and critically, it should feed its actual realized fill rates back into a monitoring layer that compares them against the backtester's capacity assumptions — if live fills are consistently worse, that's real evidence the strategy's true capacity is lower than modeled, and the fix is sizing down, not hoping the gap closes on its own.
commonMistakes: Assuming a limit order either fully fills or doesn't, rather than modeling partial fills explicitly
Not recognizing that assuming full fills near a capacity ceiling materially overstates backtested returns
Building the live execution system's partial-fill handling inconsistently with the backtester's assumptions
Not feeding live realized fill rates back into a monitoring layer that checks against the modeled capacity ceiling

questions.title: Designing a Production Fama-MacBeth Factor-Premium Pipeline
questions.prompt: Design a production pipeline that estimates and monitors factor risk premia across a firm's full factor set (market, size, value, momentum, quality) using the Fama-MacBeth procedure, running continuously as new monthly data arrives.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd structure this as two clearly separated, sequential stages running on a monthly cadence. Stage one, per-asset time-series betas: for each asset in the universe, a rolling-window regression against the full factor set is re-estimated as each new month of data arrives, with the rolling window length itself a versioned, explicit parameter (not silently changed) so betas can be reconstructed exactly for any historical date. Stage two, cross-sectional regression: for every historical month, including newly arrived ones, a cross-sectional regression of that month's returns on the betas estimated as of that month is run, producing one lambda_t per factor per month, appended to a growing, versioned time series rather than recomputed from scratch each time in a way that could silently change historical values. The final risk-premium estimate and its Fama-MacBeth standard error are computed by averaging the full lambda_t time series and taking its standard deviation divided by sqrt(T), recalculated automatically each month as new lambda_t observations arrive. For monitoring, I'd build an automated check on the trailing lambda_t series for each factor — flagging a factor whose recent-period lambda_t estimates have meaningfully diverged in sign or magnitude from its longer-run average, since that's exactly the kind of regime-dependent instability that needs human investigation rather than being silently absorbed into an ever-growing average. The entire pipeline's outputs — betas, lambda_t series, and final premium estimates — should be versioned and timestamped so that any factor-premium number reported to a PM or allocator at any point in time can be reproduced exactly from the data and parameters available as of that date.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep the two Fama-MacBeth stages cleanly separated and running on a monthly cadence: per-asset rolling betas first, versioned so they're exactly reconstructible, then a monthly cross-sectional regression appended to a growing lambda_t series rather than recomputed from scratch in a way that could quietly change history. The premium and its standard error fall out of that series automatically each month. The monitoring layer I'd insist on flags any factor whose recent lambda_t estimates have drifted meaningfully from their long-run average — that's the regime-instability signal worth a human looking at, not something that should just get smoothed into an ever-growing average unnoticed.
commonMistakes: Recomputing the entire historical lambda_t series from scratch each month rather than appending to a versioned, growing series
Not versioning the rolling-window parameter, making historical betas impossible to reconstruct exactly
Omitting an automated check for factors whose recent premia have drifted from their long-run average
Not keeping the time-series (per-asset beta) and cross-sectional (per-period premium) stages clearly separated
keyPoints: Stage one: versioned, rolling per-asset time-series betas against the full factor set, re-estimated each month
Stage two: a monthly cross-sectional regression appended to a growing, versioned lambda_t series
The final premium and Fama-MacBeth standard error are recalculated automatically as new lambda_t observations arrive
An automated monitoring check flags factors whose recent lambda_t estimates diverge meaningfully from their long-run average

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the versioned, rolling time-series beta stage
Correctly designs the appended, versioned cross-sectional lambda_t series
Correctly describes automatic recalculation of the premium and standard error
Proposes a concrete monitoring check for factor premium instability

questions.title: Designing a Capital and Liquidity Governance Structure for a Growing Broker-Dealer
questions.prompt: A broker-dealer is approaching the size and complexity where Basel-style capital and liquidity discipline (even if not formally required at its current regulatory tier) would meaningfully reduce its risk of a funding crisis. Design the internal governance structure it should adopt, including how LCR- and NSFR-style metrics would be used even without regulatory mandate.
questions.modelAnswer: Even without a regulatory mandate, I'd design the firm to voluntarily compute and monitor both an LCR-style metric (sufficient high-quality liquid assets to survive a defined short-horizon, acute stress scenario) and an NSFR-style metric (stable funding backing longer-term, less liquid assets over a one-year horizon), specifically because the two metrics catch different failure modes and the firm's own funding profile, not a regulator's threshold, is what determines its real risk. The governance structure around these metrics should follow the three-lines-of-defense model: the business lines manage their own funding and liquidity needs day to day within limits; an independent risk function (reporting separately from the business lines) sets those limits, computes and monitors both metrics against internally-set thresholds on a regular cadence, and has the authority to require corrective action — reducing less-liquid asset concentration, diversifying funding sources, extending funding tenor — well before either metric approaches a dangerous level, not only after a crisis is already underway; and an independent audit function periodically verifies the risk function is actually doing this. Critically, the firm should run its own internally-designed stress scenarios against both metrics, calibrated to its actual business (not simply copying a regulatory scenario designed for a different type or scale of institution), and a board-level risk committee should receive regular reporting on both metrics' trend over time, not just their current level, since a metric that's deteriorating even while still technically 'passing' is exactly the kind of early warning this voluntary governance structure is meant to catch before any regulator would require action.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd adopt both an LCR-style and an NSFR-style metric voluntarily, specifically because they catch different failure modes — a short, acute stress test and a longer-run funding-structure check — and the firm's actual risk doesn't care whether a regulator currently requires either one. I'd wrap both in the standard three-lines-of-defense governance: business lines operate within set limits, an independent risk function sets and monitors those limits with real authority to require corrective action, and audit periodically checks that the risk function is doing its job. The detail I'd push hardest on is reporting trend, not just current level, to the board's risk committee — a metric that's still technically fine but visibly deteriorating is exactly the early warning this whole voluntary structure exists to catch.
commonMistakes: Adopting only one of the two metrics rather than both, missing that they catch different failure modes
Designing a risk function without real independence or authority to require corrective action
Simply copying a regulatory stress scenario rather than calibrating one to the firm's actual business
Reporting only the current metric level to the board rather than its trend over time
keyPoints: Voluntarily adopting both an LCR-style and NSFR-style metric catches two distinct failure modes
A genuinely independent risk function should set limits, monitor both metrics, and have real authority for corrective action
Stress scenarios should be calibrated to the firm's actual business, not copied wholesale from a regulatory template
Board reporting should emphasize trend over time, not just current metric level, as the early-warning signal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes voluntarily adopting both LCR- and NSFR-style metrics
Correctly designs the three-lines-of-defense governance around them
Proposes firm-calibrated, not copied, stress scenarios
Correctly emphasizes trend-over-time board reporting as the early-warning mechanism

questions.title: Designing Point-in-Time Reference Data Infrastructure Across Asset Classes
questions.prompt: Design a point-in-time reference-data infrastructure for a multi-asset research platform, covering equity corporate actions, index membership changes, and fundamental data restatements, so that any historical backtest can reconstruct exactly what was knowable and investable as of any past date.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd design this around a single unifying principle applied consistently across all three data types: every fact is stored as an event with both an effective date (when it became true in the world) and a knowledge date (when it actually became available/published), never as a single current value that overwrites its own history. For equity corporate actions, every split, dividend, merger, and spin-off is a timestamped event in an append-only log, from which both raw and adjusted price series can be reconstructed as of any historical date by replaying only the events known by that date. For index membership, additions and removals are similarly stored as timestamped events, so a query for 'what was in this index on date X' replays the event log up to X rather than returning today's constituent list. For fundamental data, every reported value carries both the as-of (reporting period) date and the knowledge date it was actually published, and any subsequent restatement is stored as an entirely new, separately timestamped record rather than an overwrite of the original — so a backtest querying 'as of date X' only ever sees values whose knowledge date is on or before X, structurally incapable of returning a later restatement. Critically, I'd expose exactly one query interface across all three data types — an as-of-date query — and not expose any 'current value' endpoint to backtesting code at all, making it structurally impossible for a researcher to accidentally pull today's constituent list or today's restated fundamental value into a historical simulation, rather than relying on researchers to remember which endpoint is safe to use for backtesting. I'd pair this with automated validation that spot-checks reconstructed historical snapshots against independently-sourced historical records for a sample of dates, since the infrastructure itself needs periodic proof that its event logs are actually complete and correctly timestamped.
questions.professionalAnswer: The unifying design principle I'd apply across all three data types is: store events with both an effective date and a knowledge date, never a single current value, and expose only an as-of-date query to backtesting code — no 'current value' endpoint at all. That structural choice matters more than any documentation, because it makes pulling today's data into a historical simulation not just discouraged but actually impossible through the normal API. I'd add periodic automated validation spot-checking reconstructed historical snapshots against independent sources, because an event log that's silently incomplete or mistimed is just as dangerous as not having point-in-time data at all.
commonMistakes: Designing separate, inconsistent point-in-time mechanisms for corporate actions, index membership, and fundamental data rather than one unifying principle
Storing fundamental data restatements as overwrites rather than new, separately timestamped records
Exposing a 'current value' endpoint alongside the as-of-date query, leaving room for accidental misuse
Not including automated validation of the event logs against independent historical sources
keyPoints: A single unifying principle: every fact is a timestamped event with both an effective date and a knowledge date
Corporate actions and index membership are both append-only event logs, replayed up to any as-of date
Fundamental data restatements are new, separately timestamped records, never overwrites
Only an as-of-date query interface is exposed to backtesting code, with no 'current value' endpoint at all

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly applies a unifying event-based, knowledge-date design across all three data types
Correctly specifies restatements as new records, not overwrites
Correctly proposes exposing only an as-of-date query interface structurally
Proposes automated validation of the event logs

questions.title: Convincing an Allocator That Sharpe Alone Misses the Real Story
questions.prompt: An allocator insists on ranking three candidate managers purely by Sharpe ratio, dismissing your suggestion to also look at Calmar and Omega as 'overcomplicating a simple decision.' How do you make the case for looking deeper?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd concede directly that Sharpe is a perfectly reasonable starting point, not a flawed metric to be replaced — the case for looking further isn't that Sharpe is wrong, it's that it's incomplete, and I'd show the allocator concretely why with the candidates in front of us rather than arguing abstractly. If two managers have similar Sharpe ratios but meaningfully different max drawdowns, Calmar reveals that one of them delivers the same risk-adjusted return with a far worse worst-case experience — information the allocator, who ultimately has to live through that worst case, should want before committing capital, not after. If a manager's return distribution is meaningfully skewed (small frequent losses, rare large gains, or vice versa), Omega captures that shape directly using the full distribution, while Sharpe, built from just a mean and a standard deviation, treats a symmetric and an asymmetric return pattern with similar volatility as interchangeable when they clearly aren't experientially or risk-wise. I'd frame the extra ratios not as 'more complexity for its own sake' but as answering specific follow-up questions a single Sharpe number can't: 'how bad does my worst year actually get' and 'is this manager's risk shaped in a way I'm comfortable with' — and I'd show the actual numbers for these three specific candidates rather than making a generic argument for always using more ratios.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't argue Sharpe is the wrong number — I'd argue it's an incomplete one, and the fastest way to make that land is to show, not just assert, the gap using these three specific managers. If two of them have similar Sharpes but very different max drawdowns, that's a real difference in what it's like to actually hold the position through a bad stretch, and Calmar surfaces it directly. If one has a notably skewed return pattern, Omega catches that in a way a mean-and-variance-based ratio structurally can't. I'd frame this as answering two concrete follow-up questions the allocator actually cares about — worst-case pain and return shape — rather than as adding complexity for its own sake.
commonMistakes: Arguing that Sharpe is flawed or wrong, rather than incomplete
Making an abstract case for using more ratios rather than showing the concrete gap with these specific candidates
Not explaining specifically what Calmar and Omega each reveal that Sharpe structurally cannot
Framing the suggestion as adding complexity rather than answering a specific, relevant follow-up question
keyPoints: Sharpe is a reasonable starting point, not a metric to be dismissed as wrong
Calmar reveals worst-case drawdown differences that similar Sharpe ratios can hide
Omega captures return-distribution shape (skew) that Sharpe, built from mean and variance alone, cannot
The case should be made concretely with the actual candidates' numbers, not as an abstract argument for more complexity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames Sharpe as incomplete rather than wrong
Correctly explains what Calmar specifically reveals
Correctly explains what Omega specifically reveals
Makes the case concretely rather than abstractly

questions.title: Defending GARCH Against a Trader Who Calls It Overengineering
questions.prompt: A trader says, 'Just use the last 30 days' standard deviation for volatility — GARCH is overengineering for a problem that doesn't need it.' How do you respond, while being honest about when the trader might actually be right?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd concede the trader has a real point in some contexts before making the counter-case: for a slow-moving, low-stakes decision, a simple trailing standard deviation is genuinely fine, and reaching for GARCH there would be unnecessary complexity for no practical benefit. But I'd walk through the specific, concrete scenario where the extra complexity earns its keep: right after a sudden volatility shock, a 30-day trailing window is still mostly averaging in the calmer days before the shock, meaningfully understating current risk for days or weeks until the old data finally rolls out of the window — while GARCH's conditional variance reacts to the shock immediately through its alpha term and carries the elevated level forward through its beta term, giving a materially more accurate, responsive estimate exactly during the window that matters most for sizing and risk limits. I'd frame the actual decision criterion honestly: if the trader's use case tolerates being a few weeks slow to react to a genuine regime shift, trailing standard deviation is a reasonable, simpler choice; if the use case is sizing positions or setting risk limits where that lag could mean carrying too much risk right when it matters most, the added complexity of GARCH is justified by a concrete, measurable improvement in responsiveness, not complexity for its own sake.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd agree with the trader more than they might expect — for plenty of slower, lower-stakes uses, 30-day trailing vol is genuinely fine, and I wouldn't push GARCH just because it's more sophisticated. Where I'd push back specifically is right after a volatility shock: a 30-day window is still mostly reflecting the calm days before the shock, understating current risk for weeks, while GARCH reacts immediately and persists the new level. The honest framing is a tradeoff, not a blanket 'GARCH is always better' — if the use case can tolerate a few weeks' lag during a regime shift, trailing vol is fine; if it can't, the extra complexity earns its place.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the trader's point entirely rather than conceding it's valid in some contexts
Not identifying the specific scenario (right after a volatility shock) where the difference actually matters
Arguing GARCH is unconditionally better rather than framing this as a genuine, context-dependent tradeoff
Not explaining concretely why the trailing window lags (old calm data still in the window)
keyPoints: A simple trailing standard deviation is genuinely adequate for slower, lower-stakes use cases
The gap matters specifically right after a volatility shock, when a trailing window still reflects calmer pre-shock days
GARCH's conditional variance reacts immediately and persists the new level, unlike a trailing average
The right framing is an honest, context-dependent tradeoff, not GARCH being unconditionally superior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Honestly concedes the trader's point is valid in some contexts
Correctly identifies the specific scenario where GARCH's advantage matters
Correctly explains the mechanism behind the gap
Frames the overall answer as a genuine, non-dogmatic tradeoff

questions.title: Disclosing That a Combined Signal's Weights Were Overfit
questions.prompt: After a combined signal you built and championed goes live, you realize the IC-based combination weights were inadvertently estimated using data that overlapped with the validation period used to report the result. How do you disclose this, and what do you do immediately?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd disclose this immediately and specifically, to whoever approved the signal for live capital, rather than waiting to see if the problem resolves itself or quietly re-running the analysis correctly first and only reporting if the corrected result looks bad. I'd state plainly what happened: the combination weights were estimated on data that overlapped with what was reported as the out-of-sample validation period, which means the validation result I presented was not a genuine out-of-sample test, and the signal's true expected performance is less certain than what was originally communicated. I would not wait to deliver this news until I've already found a fix — the priority is getting the correct information in front of decision-makers as fast as possible, since live capital is currently being allocated based on a result I now know was measured incorrectly. Immediately afterward, I'd re-run the combination-weight estimation using a genuinely clean, non-overlapping train/validation split, report the corrected out-of-sample result honestly even if it's materially worse, and recommend reducing or pausing the live allocation until the corrected analysis is in hand, rather than letting the signal keep trading at its original size while the re-analysis is in progress.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go to whoever approved this for live capital immediately, not after I've quietly tried to fix it first — the fact that real money is currently sized against a result I now know wasn't a genuine out-of-sample test means the priority is getting accurate information in front of people fast, even though admitting my own mistake here is uncomfortable. I'd recommend reducing or pausing the live allocation while I re-run the analysis with a properly clean train/validation split, and whatever that corrected number comes out to, I'd report it honestly, even if it's a lot worse than what I originally presented.
commonMistakes: Waiting to disclose until after quietly re-running the analysis, delaying the correction of a decision based on bad information
Only disclosing if the corrected result turns out to be bad, rather than disclosing the methodology error regardless of outcome
Not recommending reducing or pausing the live allocation while the correct analysis is pending
Framing the disclosure defensively rather than directly and factually
keyPoints: Disclose immediately to decision-makers, not after quietly attempting to fix it first
State plainly what went wrong and what it means for the signal's actual expected performance
Recommend reducing or pausing the live allocation while the correct, clean analysis is being rerun
Report the corrected result honestly, regardless of whether it's better or worse than originally presented

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Discloses promptly and directly rather than delaying
States the error and its implications clearly and factually
Recommends reducing/pausing live allocation pending correction
Commits to reporting the corrected result honestly regardless of outcome

questions.title: Telling a Desk Head That Carry's Edge Is a Risk Premium, Not Skill
questions.prompt: A desk head wants to significantly increase sizing on a profitable carry strategy, attributing its steady returns to the team's skill in picking currency pairs. How do you reframe this conversation around what's actually driving the returns, and what it implies for sizing?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd reframe this directly but constructively: carry's steady historical profitability is best explained as compensation for a real, persistent risk premium — bearing the risk that a high-interest-rate currency depreciates less than the pure interest-rate differential implies it should, which the empirically well-documented failure of uncovered interest rate parity supports — rather than as evidence of the team's skill in selecting which currency pairs to trade. This distinction matters enormously for the sizing decision: skill-based returns, if genuinely present, tend to be relatively uncorrelated with broad market conditions and don't have an obvious, well-known failure mode; a risk premium, by contrast, is specifically compensation for bearing a risk that materializes in a correlated, sometimes sudden way — a carry crash, triggered by a broad risk-off shock, where many carry positions unwind together regardless of which specific currency pairs were chosen. I'd make the case that increasing sizing on the assumption of persistent skill, without separately budgeting for this known tail risk, understates how much the strategy could lose in exactly the scenario carry trades are known to be vulnerable to, and I'd recommend sizing the increase with that tail risk explicitly modeled and budgeted for, rather than extrapolating the steady historical returns forward as if they reflect a skill that will keep performing regardless of market regime.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate this into two different claims that get conflated easily: 'carry has been profitable' is true, but 'that profitability reflects our skill at picking pairs' is a different and much less defensible claim than 'we're being compensated for bearing a known, persistent risk that occasionally shows up as a sharp, correlated carry crash.' That distinction changes the sizing conversation completely — a genuine skill-based edge might reasonably be sized up without much more caveat, but a risk-premium-based edge needs the known tail risk explicitly budgeted for before increasing size, because the smooth historical returns are specifically the kind of pattern that masks how large the eventual correlated unwind could be.
commonMistakes: Accepting the 'skill' framing without challenging it, leading to sizing decisions that ignore the known carry-crash risk
Not explaining the specific empirical basis (the uncovered IRP failure) for the risk-premium explanation
Failing to connect the risk-premium framing to a concrete sizing recommendation (explicit tail-risk budgeting)
Delivering the reframing in a way that feels dismissive of the desk head's team rather than constructive
keyPoints: Carry's steady profitability is best explained as compensation for a persistent risk premium, not stock/pair-picking skill
This is supported by the well-documented empirical failure of uncovered interest rate parity
A risk-premium-based edge carries a known, correlated tail risk (carry crash) that a skill-based edge wouldn't necessarily share
Sizing increases should explicitly budget for this tail risk, not simply extrapolate smooth historical returns forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reframes carry's returns as a risk premium, not skill
Correctly connects this to the empirical uncovered IRP failure
Correctly explains the sizing implication (explicit tail-risk budgeting)
Delivers the reframing constructively
