questions.title: Pushing Back on Skipping Survivorship-Bias-Free Data to Save Budget
questions.prompt: Senior management, under budget pressure, proposes canceling the firm's survivorship-bias-free data subscription and switching to a cheaper, standard dataset for all future research. As the person who would have to sign off on research built on this data, how do you push back?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd push back by quantifying the decision as a risk tradeoff rather than treating it as simply a cost-saving measure, since that's genuinely what it is. I'd explain concretely that a standard dataset silently excludes every company or fund that was delisted or failed, which systematically overstates historical returns in every future backtest the firm runs on it, and that this bias compounds across every project, not just the current one under budget pressure — meaning the real cost of this decision isn't the data subscription savings, it's the risk of eventually allocating real capital to a strategy whose backtested edge was partly or entirely an artifact of this exclusion. I'd be specific about what I, as the person signing off on research, would then be unable to vouch for: any strategy built on the cheaper data going forward would carry an un-quantified, unremovable survivorship-bias risk baked into its measured historical performance, and I would not be able to responsibly approve that research for live capital with the same confidence I could today. I'd propose a concrete alternative to a flat 'yes or no' framing: quantify the actual price difference between the two data sources, and compare it honestly against even a conservative estimate of the downside risk of allocating capital to a biased result — making the tradeoff visible in dollar terms rather than letting the decision be driven purely by the smaller, more visible number (the subscription cost).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reframe this explicitly as a risk decision, not a cost-saving one, and say directly what it means for my own role: if we switch to the biased dataset, I won't be able to sign off on future research with the same confidence, because every backtest built on it will carry an unremovable, unquantified survivorship-bias risk baked into its historical performance. I'd push for putting real numbers on both sides — the actual subscription savings versus even a conservative estimate of what it costs to eventually allocate capital to a strategy whose edge was partly a data artifact — so the decision gets made with the real tradeoff visible, not just the smaller, more obvious number.
commonMistakes: Objecting in principle without quantifying the tradeoff in a way management can actually weigh
Not being specific about what this means concretely for the research sign-off process
Treating this as a one-time cost decision rather than a compounding risk across all future research
Not proposing a concrete way to compare the savings against the risk in comparable terms
keyPoints: This is a risk decision, not simply a cost-saving measure
Switching datasets bakes an unremovable survivorship-bias risk into every future backtest's results
The researcher's ability to responsibly sign off on future capital allocation is directly affected
Push for quantifying both the savings and the downside risk in comparable terms, not leaving the tradeoff implicit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reframes this as a risk decision, not just a cost decision
Correctly explains the compounding nature of the bias across future research
Articulates the concrete personal/professional stake in the sign-off process
Proposes a concrete way to make the tradeoff visible to management

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Developer on an Unrealistic Fill-Price Assumption
questions.prompt: A junior quant developer built a backtester that fills every order at the exact signal price with no slippage, and is confused about why you're asking them to change it since 'it passed all the unit tests.' How do you mentor them through this?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by validating what the unit tests actually proved: they confirmed the code does what it was written to do, correctly and reliably — that's real, valuable, and worth acknowledging. What they can't test is whether what it was written to do is itself a realistic description of how a real trade executes, and that's a separate question entirely. I'd walk through concretely why 'fills at the exact signal price' is physically impossible: the signal is computed from information available at a given moment, but by the time an order can actually reach the market, at least some time has passed and the price has almost certainly moved at least slightly — fills at the exact signal price silently assumes zero-latency, zero-impact, zero-cost execution, which doesn't exist anywhere in real markets. I'd frame the fix not as 'your code was buggy' but as 'your code is correct, and now we need to change what it's correctly modeling' — moving to a next-bar-open (or better) fill convention with slippage layered on top, and show them how to write a new test that specifically validates the new, more realistic fill logic, so they leave this conversation with both the conceptual understanding and a concrete, testable implementation path forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be careful to separate two different questions here: did the code do what it was told to do (yes, and the tests prove that), and was it told to do the right thing (no, and that's what we need to fix). Fills at the exact signal price means fills with zero latency and zero cost, which doesn't happen in any real market — I'd show concretely why, then walk through moving to a next-bar-open fill with slippage, and help them write the test that actually validates the realistic version, so this becomes a concrete skill they've built rather than just a correction they received.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the junior developer's point about passing unit tests rather than validating what the tests actually proved
Not explaining concretely and specifically why fills at the exact signal price are physically impossible
Framing the correction as 'your code was wrong' rather than 'your code is correct, now let's change what it models'
Not helping the developer build a concrete, testable path to the fix
keyPoints: Unit tests validate that code does what it was written to do, not whether what it was written to do is realistic
Fills at the exact signal price silently assume zero latency, zero impact, and zero cost, which is physically impossible
The fix should be framed as changing what correct code models, not as a bug in the code itself
Mentorship should end with a concrete, testable implementation path, not just a conceptual correction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Validates what the unit tests actually proved
Correctly and concretely explains why the fill assumption is unrealistic
Frames the correction constructively (correct code, wrong model) rather than as a mistake
Provides a concrete path forward, including a new test

questions.title: Flagging That Performance-Fee Incentives Are Driving Excess Risk-Taking
questions.prompt: You notice that a fund's '2 and 20' performance-fee structure appears to be incentivizing a specific trader to take on more risk than the fund's stated risk appetite as the measurement period's end approaches. How do you raise this, and to whom?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd raise this as a specific, evidence-based risk-governance observation, escalated to the independent risk function and senior management, not as an accusation against the individual trader — the behavior being described is a well-known, structural incentive effect of performance-fee compensation, not necessarily a sign of bad faith: a trader whose compensation is tied to crossing a high-water mark or hitting a performance threshold by a specific date has a rational, if problematic, incentive to take on more risk than usual as that date approaches, especially if they're currently below the threshold and 'need' a strong final push. I'd present concrete evidence of the pattern — specific instances where position sizing or risk-limit utilization increased near a measurement date in a way that doesn't match the trader's normal behavior — rather than a vague concern, and I'd frame the ask clearly: this is exactly the kind of risk the three-lines-of-defense structure exists to catch, and the fix isn't necessarily about this one trader, it's about whether the firm's risk limits and monitoring are robust enough to catch this incentive effect regardless of who's exhibiting it. I'd recommend the independent risk function specifically monitor risk-limit utilization in the weeks approaching performance-fee measurement dates going forward, as a standing practice, not a one-time investigation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd escalate this to the independent risk function with specific evidence, not as an accusation about one trader's character, but as a structural incentive-effect observation: performance-fee compensation tied to a measurement date creates a rational incentive to take on more risk right before that date, especially if someone's below their threshold, and that's exactly the kind of thing risk governance is supposed to catch regardless of who's doing it. I'd push for this to become a standing monitoring practice — checking risk-limit utilization specifically around measurement dates — rather than a one-off investigation of this particular instance.
commonMistakes: Framing this as an accusation against the individual trader rather than a structural incentive effect
Raising a vague concern without concrete, specific evidence of the pattern
Not escalating to the independent risk function specifically, relying instead on an informal conversation
Treating this as a one-time investigation rather than recommending a standing monitoring practice
keyPoints: Performance-fee structures create a well-known, structural incentive to take on more risk near a measurement date
This should be escalated to the independent risk function with specific, concrete evidence, not framed as an accusation
The fix is about whether firm-wide risk limits and monitoring are robust to this incentive effect generally
Recommend a standing monitoring practice around measurement dates, not just a one-time investigation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the issue as a structural incentive effect, not individual misconduct
Escalates to the correct party (independent risk function) with concrete evidence
Frames the fix around firm-wide limits/monitoring robustness
Recommends a standing, ongoing monitoring practice

questions.title: Evaluating Your Own Fit Across Researcher, Developer, and Trader Roles
questions.prompt: An interviewer asks, 'Given everything you know about quant researcher, developer, and trader roles, which would you actually choose, and why?' How do you give a genuinely thoughtful answer rather than a generic one?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd avoid a generic answer by grounding the response in the actual skill-profile differences between the three roles and being specific about which parts of my own experience and preferences map onto each: a quant researcher's work is heaviest on statistics, probability, and the discipline of rigorously testing a hypothesis without fooling yourself about overfitting — a researcher spends most of their time designing and backtesting ideas, with the research itself as the primary output, not the production system it eventually runs on. A quant developer's work is heaviest on software engineering — building and maintaining the infrastructure, data pipelines, and execution systems that the research and trading actually depend on — valuable and technically demanding in a different way, with less emphasis on originating the trading ideas themselves. A quant trader's work is heaviest on real-time market intuition and decisiveness, managing live risk and reacting to live conditions, with less time spent on the deep, patient research or infrastructure-building the other two roles require. I'd then be honest and specific about where I genuinely fit: naming concrete experiences (a specific project, a specific kind of problem I gravitated toward or found most engaging) that point toward one role over the others, rather than claiming to be equally suited to all three, which usually reads as avoiding the question rather than answering it. I'd also acknowledge, honestly, that the lines blur more at smaller firms, and that I'd be realistic about which environment size fits whichever role I named.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ground this in the real skill-profile differences rather than giving a diplomatic 'I could do any of them' answer, which usually signals to an interviewer that the candidate hasn't actually thought about it. I'd name the role I'm most drawn to specifically, backed by a concrete example from my own experience that shows why — whether that's the patient, hypothesis-driven rigor of research, the engineering discipline of building infrastructure that has to actually work in production, or the real-time decisiveness trading demands — and I'd be upfront that the lines blur at smaller firms, since pretending otherwise would undercut the honesty of the answer.
commonMistakes: Giving a generic 'I could do any of them equally well' answer that avoids actually choosing
Not grounding the choice in the specific skill-profile differences between the three roles
Not providing a concrete, specific example from personal experience supporting the choice
Failing to acknowledge that the lines between roles blur more at smaller firms
keyPoints: Quant researcher: heaviest on statistics/probability and rigorous hypothesis testing
Quant developer: heaviest on software engineering and production infrastructure
Quant trader: heaviest on real-time market intuition, decisiveness, and live risk management
A genuinely thoughtful answer names a specific choice with a concrete supporting example, not a diplomatic non-answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the three roles' skill profiles
Makes a specific, committed choice rather than a generic non-answer
Supports the choice with a concrete personal example
Acknowledges role blurring at smaller firms honestly
